title: Left Bank, Right Bank
subtitle: Two sides of the river
objectives: Compare the Left and Right Banks
Explain how soil drives the difference

steps.title: The Left Bank
steps.body: The Left Bank, west of the Garonne and Gironde, includes the Médoc and Graves. Deep gravel soils drain well and store heat, favouring Cabernet Sauvignon. The Haut-Médoc's famous communes are Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien and Margaux. Graves and Pessac-Léognan, further south, make both reds and whites.
steps.highlight: Médoc and Graves: Cabernet on gravel

steps.title: The Right Bank
steps.body: The Right Bank, north of the Dordogne, includes Saint-Émilion, Pomerol and their satellites, Fronsac and the Côtes. Cooler clay and limestone suit Merlot and Cabernet Franc. Estates are smaller and often family-run. Between the rivers, Entre-Deux-Mers makes mostly dry whites.
steps.highlight: Saint-Émilion and Pomerol: Merlot on clay

steps.prompt: Match each appellation to its bank.

steps.title: Soil and style
steps.body: Left Bank wines are often more structured, with blackcurrant, cedar and firm tannins, built for long ageing. Right Bank wines are often rounder, plummier and softer young. Saint-Émilion's limestone plateau gives freshness; Pomerol's clay gives richness. These are tendencies, not rules.

steps.prompt: Why does Cabernet Sauvignon dominate on the Left Bank?
options: Gravel soils drain and store heat, helping it ripen
steps.explanation: Gravel's warmth helps a late-ripening grape.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Left Bank's gravel favours Cabernet Sauvignon
The Right Bank's clay and limestone favour Merlot
Left Bank wines are more structured; Right Bank rounder
